question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) &=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =-\frac{1}{5}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{5}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5} & =0 \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(16,0).$

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+2 \\ y & =-x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-0+3 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,3).$

Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2 x^{2} + x$ at the point $(2,10)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,${{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(2 x^{2} + x)=4 x + 1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(2)=4 (2) + 1=9,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(9)}=- \frac{1}{9}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(10)&=- \frac{1}{9}(x-(2))\\y&=- \frac{1}{9}x+\frac{2}{9}+10\\y&=- \frac{1}{9}x+\frac{92}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{1}{9}x+\frac{92}{9}&=0\\x&=92.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(92,0).$

The normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,${{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(14 x^{2} + 7 x)=28 x + 7.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(3)=28 (3) + 7=91,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(91)}=- \frac{1}{91}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(147)&=- \frac{1}{91}(x-(3))\\y&=- \frac{1}{91}x+\frac{3}{91}+147\\y&=- \frac{1}{91}x+\frac{13380}{91}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y&=- \frac{1}{91}\cdot0+\frac{13380}{91}\\y&=\frac{13380}{91}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(0,\frac{13380}{91}).$

Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=24 x^{2} - 48 x + 40$ at the point $(2,40)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,${{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(24 x^{2} - 48 x + 40)=48 x - 48.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(2)=48 (2) - 48=48,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(48)}=- \frac{1}{48}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(40)&=- \frac{1}{48}(x-(2))\\y&=- \frac{1}{48}x+\frac{1}{24}+40\\y&=- \frac{1}{48}x+\frac{961}{24}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{1}{48}x+\frac{961}{24}&=0\\- \frac{1}{48}x&=- \frac{961}{24}\\x&=1922.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(1922,0).$

question.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(4,4)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(2\sqrt{x})=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(2 x^{\frac{1}{2}})=\frac{1}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(4)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{(4)}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2})}=-2.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(4)&=-2(x-(4))\\y&=-2x+8+4\\y&=-2x+12.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y&=-2\cdot0+12\\y&=12.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(0,12).$

$$

$$

The normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,${{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(24\sqrt[3]{x^{2}})=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(24 x^{\frac{2}{3}})=\frac{16}{x^{\frac{1}{3}}}=\frac{16}{\sqrt[3]{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=\frac{16}{\sqrt[3]{(1)}}=16,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(16)}=- \frac{1}{16}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(24)&=- \frac{1}{16}(x-(1))\\y&=- \frac{1}{16}x+\frac{1}{16}+24\\y&=- \frac{1}{16}x+\frac{385}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y&=- \frac{1}{16}\cdot0+\frac{385}{16}\\y&=\frac{385}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(0,\frac{385}{16}).$

The normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,${{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(14\sqrt[4]{x})=14\cdot\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(x^{1/4})=14\cdot\frac{1}{4}x^{-3/4}=\frac{7}{2 x^{\frac{3}{4}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=\frac{7}{2 (1)^{\frac{3}{4}}}=\frac{7}{2},
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(\frac{7}{2})}=- \frac{2}{7}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(14)&=- \frac{2}{7}(x-(1))\\y&=- \frac{2}{7}x+\frac{2}{7}+14\\y&=- \frac{2}{7}x+\frac{100}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y&=- \frac{2}{7}\cdot0+\frac{100}{7}\\y&=\frac{100}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(0,\frac{100}{7}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\frac{2}{x}+1)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(1 + \frac{2}{x})=- \frac{2}{x^{2}}=- \frac{2}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=- \frac{2}{(1)^{2}}=-2,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-2)}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(3)&=\frac{1}{2}(x-(1))\\y&=\frac{1}{2}x- \frac{1}{2}+3\\y&=\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{2}&=0\\x&=-5.\end{aligned}

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(-5,0).$

The normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,${{field-2}}$).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(\frac{16}{x}+8)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(8 + \frac{16}{x})=- \frac{16}{x^{2}}=- \frac{16}{x^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=- \frac{16}{(1)^{2}}=-16,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-16)}=\frac{1}{16}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(24)&=\frac{1}{16}(x-(1))\\y&=\frac{1}{16}x- \frac{1}{16}+24\\y&=\frac{1}{16}x+\frac{383}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y&=\frac{1}{16}\cdot0+\frac{383}{16}\\y&=\frac{383}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(0,\frac{383}{16}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x) &=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(2 x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 4 x)=-4 + \frac{1}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=-4 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=-4 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1)}}=-3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-3)}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2)&=\frac{1}{3}(x-(1))\\y&=\frac{1}{3}x- \frac{1}{3}-2\\y&=\frac{1}{3}x- \frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x- \frac{7}{3}&=0\\\frac{1}{3}x&=\frac{7}{3}\\x&=7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$
